sense: of a book, poem or work

evidence: Ov. Rem. 1: titulum nōmenque libellī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The usual word for a book’s title from Augustus on. Lewis & Short’s other senses: an inscription or epitaph, a label on a jar or a slave put up for sale, a notice that a house is for sale or to let (Plin. Ep. 7.27.7), and, figuratively, a title of honour (see title, of a person) or a pretext.

terms.gloss: title (what is written on a book); an inscription
terms.comment: Cicero’s word for the title of his De officiis. Properly “a writing on”, so also an inscription on a monument (Plin. NH 29.11) or a brand on a slave’s forehead (Petr.).

terms.gloss: to entitle; liber īnscrībitur, the book is called
terms.comment: Cicero’s way of giving a title: in eō librō, quī Oeconomicus īnscrībitur (Off. 2.87).

terms.gloss: title; the title tag hung on a book roll
evidence: Cic. de Orat. 2.61: dēceptus indicibus librōrum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The strip of parchment that carried a roll’s title, Greek σίλλυβος (Cic. Att. 4.4a.1), and so the title itself (Suet. Cal. 49, Liv. 38.56). Its everyday senses are others: a pointer, the forefinger, an informer, a list (see index, in a book).

phrases.latin: Sed dē amīcitiā aliō librō dictum est, quī īnscrībitur Laelius.
phrases.english: But friendship has been dealt with in another book, which is entitled Laelius.

phrases.latin: quod dē īnscrīptiōne quaeris, nōn dubitō quīn καθῆκον officium sit, nisi quid tū aliud; sed īnscrīptiō plēnior dē officiīs.
phrases.english: As for your question about the title: I have no doubt that καθῆκον is officium, unless you think otherwise; but the fuller title is De officiis.

phrases.latin: iīsque imperēs ut sūmant membrānulam ex quā indicēs fīant, quōs vōs Graecī, ut opīnor, σιλλύβους appellātis.
phrases.english: and tell them to get a bit of parchment to make the title tags, which you Greeks, I think, call sillyboi.
